opus-5.5.text:
I think it's not only feasible, it's probably necessary if we want robot learning to scale. The fundamental bottleneck right now is data. Teleoperation gives you very high-quality, embodiment-matched data, but it's slow, expensive, and it doesn't scale the way internet text or images did for language and vision models. Humans, on the other hand, are doing manipulation tasks all day, every day, in incredibly diverse environments. If we can capture even a fraction of that, it's an enormous source of signal.

That said, there's a real gap we have to take seriously: the embodiment gap. A human hand is not a parallel-jaw gripper. Our kinematics, our sensing, the way we move our head and eyes, all of that differs from a robot. So you can't just take a video of a person and expect a policy to copy it directly. The question becomes: what parts of human behavior actually transfer?

My view is that a lot of the high-level structure transfers really well: where to look, what objects matter, the sequence of subgoals, the rough trajectory of the hand through space. The low-level details, like exact contact forces or finger configurations, transfer less directly. So in our work we've been thinking about how to design the data collection and the representation so they're aligned from the start. For example, using egocentric devices like wearable glasses that roughly match the robot's camera viewpoint, tracking hand poses in 3D, and then treating human data and robot data as two embodiments that share a common action space, rather than as totally separate things.

What we've seen is that co-training on a large amount of human data plus a smaller amount of robot data can significantly improve generalization, to new scenes, new object arrangements, sometimes even new tasks, compared to training on robot data alone. The human data gives you breadth, and the robot data grounds it in the actual physical embodiment.

So I'd frame it this way: human data won't completely replace robot data, at least not soon. But I think it can become the bulk of the data, the foundation, with robot data acting as the calibration layer on top. And as hardware gets more humanlike and our capture tools get better, that gap will keep shrinking.

r001.rationale: It proposes tracking human hand poses in 3D and representing human and robot data in a shared action space, making human movement usable for robot learning.

r002.rationale: It identifies transferable perceptual information such as where to look and which objects matter, and proposes egocentric capture aligned with the robot’s camera viewpoint.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says to treat human data and robot data as two embodiments sharing a common action space, framing the human as another embodiment for this purpose.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So this is a question I get asked a lot, and my honest answer is that I'm both excited and somewhat skeptical, depending on what exactly you mean by "directly."

The appeal is obvious. If you look at why language models and vision models took off, it's because the internet handed us essentially free supervision at a scale no lab could ever collect on its own. Robotics doesn't have that. Every demonstration we collect with teleoperation costs us human time, robot time, and a lot of maintenance. So people look at the billions of hours of video of humans doing things with their hands and say, that's the internet-scale dataset for robots. And at a high level, I agree that's where the leverage has to come from eventually.

But the word "directly" is where it breaks down for me. Human video is not robot data. There are at least three gaps you have to close. The first is the embodiment gap. A human hand has twenty-something degrees of freedom, compliant skin, incredible tactile sensing. Most robot hands are two-finger grippers or, at best, a fairly stiff multi-fingered hand. The strategies a human uses, say rolling an object in the palm or using the fingers as a cage, often just don't transfer as a motor command. The second is the observation gap. A human video is shot from some arbitrary viewpoint, usually with the person's body in it, and the robot sees the world from its own cameras with its own arm in the frame. The third, and I think the most underappreciated, is the action gap. Video gives you what happened, not the control signal that caused it. There are no joint torques, no gripper commands. You're inferring intent from pixels, and that inference is noisy exactly in the fine-grained moments, like the instant of contact, where robots fail most.

So where do I think human data actually helps? I think it's most useful not as training data for the low-level policy, but as a source of what I'd call priors. Things like what the task structure is, what sequence of subgoals makes sense, where the hand should be in the scene, how objects move when manipulated. You can learn representations and even world models from human video, and those can make the robot-specific learning much more sample-efficient. We've seen this in our own work and others': pretrain on human video, then fine-tune on a comparatively small amount of robot data, and the gains are real. But notice that the robot data is still in the loop. It's doing the grounding.

There's also been a lot of progress on the retargeting side, taking a human hand pose and mapping it onto a robot hand, and that's gotten good enough that for some tasks you can bootstrap a policy almost entirely from human motion. I think that's genuinely promising, especially for dexterous hands where teleoperation is painful anyway. But the moment the task depends on contact dynamics, on how much force to apply, on recovering when something slips, the retargeted human motion becomes a starting point rather than a solution, and you need either real-world rollouts or very good simulation to close the loop.

So if I had to summarize my position: I don't think of human data as robot data. I think of it as the thing that tells the robot what to try and roughly how, and I think the field would be better off being precise about that distinction rather than hoping the gap just disappears with scale. It might shrink with scale. But right now the places where it doesn't shrink are exactly the hard parts of manipulation, and those are the parts I care about.

r001.rationale: The response describes retargeting human hand poses onto robot hands and bootstrapping policies from human motion, identifying movement conversion as an enabling step.

r002.rationale: It discusses the observation gap and learning representations from human video, but does not identify converting human perception into robot-usable policy inputs.

r003.rationale: The response emphasizes differences between human and robot embodiment; it does not frame a human as another robot.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a really promising direction, but I wouldn’t say human data is directly interchangeable with robot data. If you watch a person make coffee, you can learn a lot about the task: which objects matter, the order of the steps, and what success looks like. But that video doesn’t necessarily tell a robot how to move its own arm, how much force to apply, or whether it has a stable grasp.

So I think the key question is what we want to transfer. Human data can provide a lot of the task understanding, while robot experience helps ground that understanding in the robot’s own body and actions. The exciting possibility is that you don’t have to learn everything from robot data anymore. You can use human demonstrations to get much of the way there, and then use robot data to learn the parts that depend on actually interacting with the world.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning task understanding from human demonstrations, but does not identify converting human perception into robot-usable policy inputs.

r003.rationale: The response says human data is not directly interchangeable with robot data; it does not frame a human as another robot.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very promising, but it depends on what you want the robot to learn from the human data. If you want it to learn what a task looks like—what objects matter, what steps need to happen, what success looks like—human video can provide a lot of useful information. But if you want to use that video directly to tell a robot how to move, there’s a much bigger gap. Our hands, our bodies, and the way we interact with the world are different from a robot’s.

There’s also information that’s hard to recover just by watching. You can see someone picking up a cup, but you don’t necessarily know how much force they’re applying or exactly when they make contact. Those details matter for control.

So I think the opportunity is to learn broadly from human data and then use robot experience to connect that knowledge to actions the robot can actually execute. The question is how much robot data you need to make that connection, and how well it generalizes to new tasks.

r001.rationale: It describes a gap between human video and robot movement, then says robot experience can connect learned knowledge to actions the robot can execute.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning task information from human video, but does not identify converting human perception into robot-usable policy inputs.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes differences between human bodies and robots; it does not frame a human as another robot.
